question: In the middle of a Claude Code session you run `/clear`. What does it do?
options: Deletes the project's CLAUDE.md file so Claude forgets the project instructions
Redraws the terminal screen but keeps the whole conversation intact
Wipes the current conversation context and starts you fresh in the same directory
Logs you out so you have to re-authenticate before the next prompt
explanation: `/clear` resets the conversation: the next turn is assembled with none of the previous back-and-forth, as if you had just launched a new session in the same project. This matters because of the stateless loop — every turn resends the entire conversation to the API, so a long history means every new turn costs more and eats more of the context window. `/clear` is the cheapest way to drop that baggage when you switch tasks. It does not touch files on disk (CLAUDE.md survives, and the old transcript is still saved and resumable), which is why the CLAUDE.md option is wrong. Redrawing the screen is a different action (Ctrl+L), and authentication is unrelated — especially on Bedrock, where auth comes from AWS credentials, not a session login.

question: You want to switch to a different Claude model for the rest of your current session. Which slash command do you use?
options: /model
/config
/switch
/init
explanation: `/model` changes which model the harness will call for subsequent turns of the current session. Because the loop is stateless — the harness resends the whole conversation on every turn — switching models mid-session simply means the next resend goes to a different model; nothing that already happened is re-run. `/config` opens general settings and can set a default, but `/model` is the direct in-session switch. `/switch` is not a real command, and `/init` does something entirely different (it generates a CLAUDE.md for the project). One Bedrock-flavored note: when running through Bedrock, the models you can pick must be ones enabled in your AWS account and region, and model identifiers there are Bedrock model IDs or inference profiles rather than plain Anthropic API names.

question: A teammate who runs Claude Code against AWS Bedrock asks why they've never needed `/login`. What's the accurate answer?
options: Bedrock users authenticate through /login too, but the OAuth token it stores stays valid for twelve months, so they only did it once and forgot
With CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK set, auth comes from the standard AWS credential chain, so there's no Anthropic account login step
Claude Code disables all authentication when talking to Bedrock because the traffic stays inside your VPC and never crosses the public internet
/login is only required for the -p headless mode, which they apparently never use
explanation: `/login` exists to connect Claude Code to an Anthropic account — either a Claude subscription via OAuth or a Console API key. When `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK` is set, requests go to AWS instead, and they're signed with whatever the standard AWS credential chain provides: environment variables, an AWS profile, an IAM role, SSO, etc. There is simply no Anthropic-side account in the picture, so the login step doesn't apply. The 'only once' option is wrong because Bedrock users never run it at all. The VPC option confuses network topology with authentication — Bedrock requests are still authenticated, just with AWS SigV4 credentials rather than an Anthropic token. And `/login` has nothing to do with `-p`; headless and interactive modes use the same auth resolution.

question: What is the key difference between `/compact` and `/clear`?
options: /compact deletes old transcript JSONL files from ~/.claude/ to reclaim disk space, while /clear only hides them from the current session view
/clear summarizes the conversation into a shorter form so context survives; /compact throws the whole conversation away and starts from zero
/compact is automatic-only and cannot be invoked manually, unlike /clear
/compact replaces the conversation with a summary so work can continue with context; /clear drops the conversation entirely
explanation: Both commands attack the same problem — the resend grows every turn, so a long conversation gets expensive and eventually hits the context window. `/compact` asks the model to summarize the conversation so far, then continues with that summary (plus a recent tail) in place of the full history: you keep working memory of the task at a fraction of the tokens. `/clear` is the blunt version: it discards the conversation entirely, keeping nothing. Note that compaction itself costs a full read of the conversation, since the model must ingest everything to summarize it. The second option has the two commands reversed. Neither touches transcript files on disk — the session record survives both. And compaction runs automatically near the context limit, but `/compact` exists precisely so you can trigger it manually at a moment you choose.

question: What is plan mode in Claude Code for?
options: Having Claude research the task and propose an approach before it is allowed to change anything
Scheduling a session to run later at a planned time
Making Claude respond faster by planning several turns in advance
Splitting the work across multiple parallel subagents, each assigned one step of a pre-drafted plan before execution begins
explanation: Plan mode restricts Claude to read-only exploration: it can search, read files, and reason, but it can't edit files or run state-changing commands. Instead it produces a plan for you to review; only after you approve does it proceed to execute. The mechanism is a permission mode — the harness withholds approval for mutating tools, which is why this is enforced reliably rather than being a polite request in the prompt. It's the right mode when the change is risky or ambiguous and you want to sanity-check the approach before any file is touched. The distractors misread the word 'plan': there's no scheduling feature by that name, no multi-turn lookahead for speed, and while multi-agent workflows exist, plan mode itself is about gating execution behind your approval, not about parallelism.

question: You switch Claude Code into auto-accept (acceptEdits) mode. What changes compared to the default mode?
options: Claude stops asking for your confirmation on anything at all, including arbitrary shell commands and file deletions
Claude automatically accepts and submits your typed prompts without you having to press Enter to confirm each one
File edits are applied without a permission prompt each time, instead of asking you to approve each one
Claude switches to a faster model to keep up with the accepted edits
explanation: In the default mode, the harness pauses before each file edit (and other gated actions) and asks you to approve. acceptEdits mode pre-approves file edits specifically, so Claude can write and modify files without stopping — useful when you trust the direction and don't want to click through dozens of small changes. Crucially, it is not a blanket 'yes to everything': commands and other tools that would normally prompt can still prompt. That's the difference from bypassPermissions, which the first option is describing. The permission check happens in the harness, on your machine, before the tool runs — the model itself never executes anything; it only emits tool-use requests that the harness decides to honor. Mode changes never affect which model is used or how your input is submitted.

question: Which set correctly names Claude Code's core permission modes?
options: readonly, readwrite, admin, root
default, acceptEdits, plan, bypassPermissions
safe, balanced, fast, unrestricted
manual, assisted, supervised, autonomous
explanation: The core permission modes are `default` (prompt for approval on gated actions), `acceptEdits` (file edits pre-approved), `plan` (read-only research, propose before acting), and `bypassPermissions` (no prompts at all — for isolated or throwaway environments only). You cycle through available modes with Shift+Tab in the interactive UI, and can start a session in a given mode with the `--permission-mode` flag or set it in settings.json. The mode names matter beyond trivia because they appear verbatim in configuration. The other option sets are invented vocabularies: they sound like plausible product tiers but match nothing in the harness. Note what a permission mode actually is: a policy applied by the harness on your machine when the model requests a tool — it changes nothing about the API request itself, so it works identically on Bedrock and on the Anthropic API.

question: What distinguishes bypassPermissions mode from acceptEdits mode?
options: bypassPermissions can only be set per-project in .claude/settings.json, while acceptEdits can only be enabled per-user in ~/.claude/settings.json
acceptEdits auto-approves file edits and shell commands alike, while bypassPermissions covers only file edits but also suppresses the confirmation dialog
They behave identically; bypassPermissions is just the legacy name for acceptEdits
acceptEdits auto-approves file edits only, while bypassPermissions skips permission prompting entirely, including for shell commands
explanation: acceptEdits removes the prompt for one category — file edits — while everything else still goes through the normal permission flow. bypassPermissions removes the prompting layer altogether: any tool the model requests, including arbitrary Bash commands, runs without asking. That's why it's paired with the deliberately scary `--dangerously-skip-permissions` flag and is meant for sandboxed or disposable environments (like CI containers), not for a session on your workstation with real credentials lying around. The second option inverts the two modes. They are certainly not aliases — the whole point of having both is the difference in blast radius. And either mode can be set for a session regardless of where settings live; the modes themselves aren't tied to user-vs-project scoping. Remember the model only ever emits tool-use requests; permission modes decide how much of that the harness honors without you in the loop.

question: Claude is midway through a long response and heading in the wrong direction. Which key stops it so you can redirect?
options: Esc
Ctrl+Z
Ctrl+D
F5
explanation: Esc interrupts Claude mid-turn: the current response or tool call stops, but the work completed so far in the session is kept, and you can immediately type a correction. This is the everyday steering tool — interrupting early is far cheaper than letting a wrong approach run to completion, because every subsequent turn resends the whole (now longer) conversation. The others do different things: Ctrl+Z suspends the entire Claude Code process to your shell (Unix job control — you'd run `fg` to come back), Ctrl+D exits the session, and F5 isn't bound. Worth knowing the neighbors too: Ctrl+C clears the input or exits, and double-Esc on an empty prompt opens the rewind menu to restore an earlier point in the session rather than just stopping the current one.

question: Which keyboard shortcut cycles between permission modes (default → acceptEdits → plan …) during an interactive session?
options: Ctrl+P
Tab
Shift+Tab
Ctrl+M
explanation: Shift+Tab cycles through the permission modes available in your session — default (shown as 'Manual' in the mode indicator), acceptEdits, plan, and any extra modes you've enabled. It's the fastest way to hop into plan mode before a risky request or into auto-accept for a long mechanical refactor, without touching configuration files. The distractors are all real-feeling but wrong: plain Tab is used for completions and accepting suggestions, Ctrl+P moves through command history (like the Up arrow), and Ctrl+M isn't a mode toggle. A useful mental separation: shortcuts like this only change harness-side behavior — what the harness will auto-approve — and have zero effect on the API request itself, so the model doesn't 'know' which mode you're in except through what the harness tells it (for example, the constraints of plan mode).

question: You type `!git status` at the Claude Code prompt. What happens?
options: Claude is asked to run `git status` on your behalf and must first request permission for the Bash tool as with any command
The input is rejected because `!` is reserved for history expansion
Claude Code opens a persistent interactive subshell that replaces the session prompt until you type exit to return
The command runs directly in your shell, and its output is added to the session so Claude can see it
explanation: The `!` prefix enters shell mode: the command executes immediately on your machine without going through the model at all, and both the command and its output are appended to the session context. That last part is the trick worth knowing — because the harness resends the whole conversation each turn, the output becomes visible to Claude on your next prompt, so `!` is a fast way to feed it fresh ground truth (test results, git state) without asking it to run the command itself. The first option describes the normal, non-prefixed path where the model chooses to call Bash and the permission system gets involved; `!` skips both the model and the prompt since you ran it yourself. History expansion with `!` is disabled by default, and there's no session-replacing subshell — each `!` line is one command.

question: You want to write a multi-line prompt in Claude Code, and it must work in any terminal without extra configuration. Which input inserts a newline instead of submitting?
options: Shift+Enter, which is guaranteed native in every terminal
Typing a backslash and then pressing Enter
Ctrl+Enter, the universal newline binding
Pressing Enter twice quickly
explanation: The backslash-then-Enter 'quick escape' works in all terminals with no setup (Ctrl+J is the other universally available option). The reason terminal support even matters: many terminals send Shift+Enter as a plain Enter, so Claude Code can't distinguish them without help. Shift+Enter does work natively in a good list of modern terminals (iTerm2, Ghostty, Kitty, Windows Terminal, and others), but in environments like the VS Code integrated terminal you first run `/terminal-setup` to install the binding — so 'guaranteed everywhere' is exactly what it isn't. Option+Enter is another route on macOS but requires configuring Option as Meta. Ctrl+Enter isn't the binding, and double-Enter would just submit your first line. This is worth knowing cold, because a submitted half-prompt still becomes a full turn — resent conversation, real tokens, real cost.

question: You run `/init` in a repository that Claude Code has never seen. What does it do?
options: Explores the codebase and generates a CLAUDE.md file documenting the project for future sessions
Runs `git init`, writes a language-appropriate .gitignore, and creates an initial commit on your behalf
Creates the ~/.claude directory scaffold, including a default global settings.json and an empty skills folder
Registers the project with your Anthropic account so usage is billed to it
explanation: `/init` has Claude explore the repository — build commands, structure, conventions — and write what it learns into a CLAUDE.md at the project root. The payoff comes from how CLAUDE.md is used afterward: the harness injects it into the prompt of every future session in that project, so it's the durable memory layer in an otherwise stateless system. Nothing lives server-side between sessions; a file the harness re-reads and resends is how 'the project's knowledge' persists. It is unrelated to `git init` — Claude Code doesn't initialize repositories as part of `/init` — and `~/.claude/` global scaffolding is created by the CLI itself, not this command. The billing option doesn't correspond to anything real; and for a Bedrock user there's no Anthropic account registration in the picture at all — usage lands on the AWS bill.

question: What does the built-in `/review` command do?
options: Replays the current session's transcript so you can review what Claude did
Shows a diff of every file Claude has modified since the session started
Has Claude review a pull request and give feedback on the changes
Audits your settings.json and permission rules for risky configuration
explanation: `/review` points Claude at a pull request: it fetches the PR's changes (typically via the `gh` CLI), reads the diff in context, and produces review feedback — the kind of task that plays to an agent's strength of reading many files to judge one change. It's a packaged workflow: you could prompt the same thing by hand, but the command bundles the steps. The distractors each map to a different real surface, which is what makes them tempting: reviewing what Claude did in-session is the transcript view (Ctrl+O), file changes are visible through git itself since Claude edits your working tree directly, and configuration checks are territory for `/doctor` and `/permissions`, not `/review`. Provider-wise this is fully neutral — the review runs through whatever model endpoint you've configured, Bedrock or Anthropic, since the command is just harness-side orchestration.

question: What is the key operational difference between a skill and a slash command in Claude Code?
options: Skills run locally inside the harness process, while slash commands are executed server-side by the API before the response streams back
Slash commands are built-in and cannot be user-defined, whereas skills are the only supported way for users to add custom behavior
Skills can call tools but slash commands cannot
A slash command is invoked explicitly by the user; a skill can be triggered by the model when its description matches the task
explanation: The distinction is who pulls the trigger. A slash command fires only when you type it — deterministic, user-driven. A skill advertises itself via a short description that sits in the model's context; when the model judges that the current task matches, it loads the skill's full instructions and follows them. That's why writing a good skill description matters so much: it's the trigger condition. The mechanism also explains the cost profile — descriptions are always carried in the resent context, bodies only on activation. The first option misplaces the machinery: both are harness-side; the API server executes nothing (a useful invariant on Bedrock and Anthropic alike). The second is false because custom slash commands are fully supported alongside skills. And both paths can lead to tool use — a command's prompt or a skill's instructions can each have Claude invoke tools.

question: You want Claude to permanently remember a project convention ('we use tabs, never spaces') across all future sessions. What's the supported way?
options: Tell Claude once in a session; the model updates its weights with your preference
Add it to the project's CLAUDE.md, for example via the /memory command
Set it as an environment variable so the API includes it in every request
Enable the conversation-sync option so future sessions download past chats
explanation: Persistent memory in Claude Code is a file. CLAUDE.md (project-level, or user-level in ~/.claude/ for personal preferences) is read by the harness and injected into the prompt at the start of every session — that's the entire mechanism. `/memory` opens these files for editing so you don't have to hunt for them. The first option is the classic misconception this topic exists to kill: model weights are frozen; nothing you say in a session trains the model, and the API keeps no state between requests — every turn is a full resend of what the harness chose to include. Environment variables configure the harness (model choice, Bedrock routing) but their values aren't injected as instructions into prompts. And there is no conversation-sync feature; past transcripts exist locally and can be resumed, but new sessions don't automatically inherit old conversations — CLAUDE.md is the designed channel for durable knowledge.

question: What does running `claude -p "summarize the failing tests"` do differently from just running `claude`?
options: It runs headless: processes the single prompt, prints the result to stdout, and exits instead of opening the interactive UI
It runs the prompt in plan mode, printing a proposed step-by-step plan to stdout for your approval before anything executes
It runs the prompt with elevated permissions, skipping all confirmation prompts
It pipes the prompt into the most recently used session for this directory and reattaches your terminal to that conversation
explanation: `-p` (`--print`) is headless mode: Claude Code takes the prompt from the command line, runs the full agentic loop — including tool calls — non-interactively, writes the final result to stdout, and exits. That makes it composable in shells and CI: pipe input in, capture output, chain with `--output-format json` for machine-readable results. The full harness machinery still applies (same context assembly, same permission rules — which is why CI usage often pairs it with explicit `--allowedTools`). The 'p' tempts people toward 'plan', but plan mode is a permission mode (`--permission-mode plan`), not this flag. It doesn't elevate permissions — that misconception would make `-p` dangerous, and it's the separate, deliberately verbose `--dangerously-skip-permissions` flag. And it starts a fresh conversation unless you explicitly combine it with `--continue` or `--resume`.

question: What is the difference between `claude --continue` and `claude --resume`?
options: --continue reopens a session that crashed or was killed mid-turn, recovering its state from disk; --resume reopens one you exited cleanly with Ctrl+D
--continue keeps the conversation history but resets permission decisions to your settings defaults; --resume preserves both the conversation and the grants
--continue loads the most recent conversation in the current directory; --resume lets you pick a specific past session by ID, name, or from a picker
They are aliases; --resume is simply the long form of --continue
explanation: `--continue` (`-c`) is the zero-decision path: it reopens the most recent conversation for the directory you're in. `--resume` (`-r`) is the targeted path: give it a session ID or name, or run it bare to get an interactive picker of past sessions. Both work because every session's conversation is persisted locally as a transcript (JSONL under ~/.claude/) — resuming means the harness reloads that record and resends it as the conversation history on your next turn. Nothing was ever stored server-side, so 'resuming' is purely a local-file operation; this is the stateless loop again, and it behaves identically on Bedrock and the Anthropic API. They aren't aliases, the clean-vs-crashed distinction doesn't exist (either can reopen either), and neither flag touches permission state — permissions re-resolve from your settings whenever a session starts.

question: What does setting the environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1 actually change?
options: It downloads a distilled copy of the Claude model weights into your AWS account so the CLI can run inference locally through SageMaker
The harness routes its model API calls to Amazon Bedrock, authenticated via your AWS credentials, instead of the Anthropic API
It switches the CLI binary to a special AWS build with different commands
It enables AWS-specific tools inside the session, such as an S3 browser and a CloudWatch log reader for debugging deployed services
explanation: The flag changes one thing: the destination and signing of API requests. With it set, the same harness sends its (Anthropic-shaped) requests to the Bedrock endpoint in your configured AWS region, signed with credentials from the standard AWS chain — env vars, a profile, an IAM role. Everything above that layer is untouched: same CLI, same slash commands, same tools, same permission system, and the same Claude model weights answering — Bedrock is a different door to the same model, hosted by AWS. That's why the weights-download option is wrong twice over: no weights ever leave the provider, on either path. There's no separate AWS build of the CLI, and no bonus AWS tools appear in the session. Practical corollaries: `/login` becomes irrelevant, model selection uses Bedrock model IDs or inference profiles, and cost shows up on the AWS bill rather than an Anthropic console.

question: You're scripting Claude Code in CI with `claude -p` and want machine-readable output. Which values does `--output-format` accept?
options: yaml, json, and xml
plain, rich, and raw
markdown, html, and json
text, json, and stream-json
explanation: `--output-format` in print mode accepts `text` (the default final answer as plain text), `json` (a single structured result including metadata like cost and session ID — the one you usually want in CI, parsed with something like jq), and `stream-json` (newline-delimited JSON events emitted as the run progresses, useful for observing the loop live: each tool call and message appears as its own event). The stream variant is a window into the agentic loop itself — you can watch the turn-by-turn tool round-trips that are normally rendered as UI. The other option sets are plausible-sounding format families that the flag doesn't offer; markdown is how Claude tends to write text, not an output-format value. This is provider-neutral: output formatting happens entirely in the harness after responses come back, so it works identically whether the endpoint behind it is Bedrock or the Anthropic API.
